title: Exceptions
summary: Catch the failures you can handle, throw the ones you cannot, and never hide an error.

steps.title: When a line cannot do its job
body: `int.Parse("abc")` cannot return a number. So it does not return at all. It **throws an exception**: an object describing what went wrong.
A thrown exception abandons the current line and travels back up through the methods that called it, looking for someone prepared to deal with it. If nobody is, the program crashes.
`try` and `catch` are how you say *I am prepared*:
- The moment a line in the `try` block throws, the **rest of the block is skipped**.
- If the exception's type matches the `catch`, that block runs.
- Afterwards the program continues below, as if nothing had happened.

steps.prompt: Follow the jump. What does this print?
steps.explain: `int.Parse("x")` throws, so `B` is never reached. Control jumps to the `catch`, then carries on after the whole `try`/`catch`.

steps.title: The exception object, and finally
body: Give the exception a name and you can read what it says:

A `finally` block runs **whatever happens**: when the `try` succeeds, when an exception is caught, and even when an exception flies past uncaught. It is the place for clean-up that must not be skipped, such as closing a file or releasing a lock.
You can also stack several `catch` blocks. C# tries them **top to bottom** and runs the first one whose type matches, so the most specific type goes first.

steps.prompt: Parse the input. If it is not a number, use 0. Print `Done` whatever happens.
steps.explain: The order of the blocks is fixed: `try`, then any `catch` blocks, then `finally` last.

steps.title: Throwing your own
body: You have been throwing since the constructors lesson. Now the full picture.
throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException("amount", "Amount must be positive");
Checks at the top of a method like these are called **guard clauses**. Fail early, before anything has been changed.
Pick the type that tells the caller what kind of mistake it was:
| `ArgumentException` | a value you passed is not acceptable |
| `ArgumentNullException` | you passed null where it is not allowed |
| `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` | the value is outside the allowed range |
| `InvalidOperationException` | the object is in the wrong state for this call |
| `FormatException` | text was not in the expected format |
The last two `Argument...` types inherit from `ArgumentException`, so a `catch (ArgumentException)` catches all three.

steps.prompt: `SetDiscount(int percent)` only accepts 0 to 100. A caller passes 250. Which exception fits best?
steps.explain: The argument itself is the problem, and specifically its range. `InvalidOperationException` is for a good argument at a bad time. `NullReferenceException` is one you should never throw yourself: it means a bug.

steps.title: A forgiving quantity box
prompt: Write a method `int ParseQuantity(string text)` for a quantity field on an order form.
- text that is a whole number returns that number: `"12"` gives `12`
- text that is **not** a number returns `0`: catch the `FormatException` that `int.Parse` throws
- a **negative** number is a mistake the caller must hear about: throw `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`
Use `int.Parse` with `try` and `catch` here. (There is a neater tool for this exact job, and it is two lessons away.)
solution: throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException("text", "Quantity cannot be negative");

forbid.message: Does not use TryParse (that comes later)

hints: Declare `int quantity;` before the `try`, so it is still visible after it.
After the `try`/`catch`, check `if (quantity < 0) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException("text", "...");` and then return the quantity.

steps.title: Custom exceptions
body: The built-in types describe programming mistakes well. They do not describe **your business**. When a failure has a meaning in your domain, and data a caller might want, give it its own type.
An exception is just a class that inherits from `Exception`:
public OutOfStockException(string sku) : base($"{sku} is out of stock")
- The name ends in `Exception` by convention.
- `: base(...)` passes the text up, and it becomes `Message`.
- Extra properties carry the facts. The caller can read `ex.Sku` instead of picking apart a sentence.

steps.prompt: Complete the custom exception, then throw one.
steps.explain: Inherit from `Exception`, hand the message to the base constructor, and raise it with `throw new`.

steps.title: Filters, and never swallow
body: A `catch` can carry a condition. `when` means *catch this type, but only if this is also true*:
Now the rule that matters more than any syntax. This is the worst code in this lesson:
It catches **everything**, including bugs you have never imagined, and does **nothing**. The charge failed, the program says it is fine, and the evidence is gone.
- Catch the **specific** types you know how to handle.
- If you cannot handle it here, do not catch it. Let it travel up to code that can.
- If you only want to note it and pass it on, write `throw;` on its own inside the `catch`. That rethrows the same exception.

steps.prompt: The first `catch` that matches wins. What does this print?
code: public PaymentException(int code) : base($"Payment failed with code {code}")
steps.explain: The first filter is false for 402, so that `catch` is skipped. The second matches. Only one `catch` ever runs, and `finally` runs regardless.

steps.title: A wallet that explains itself
prompt: Write a custom exception and a class that throws, catches and cleans up.
- `Message` is `"Short by "` followed by the shortfall, for example `"Short by 12"`
- `Balance` and `Attempts` (`int`): readable by anyone, settable only inside the class

- `void Pay(decimal amount)`: throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` when the amount is zero or negative; throws `InsufficientFundsException` carrying how much is missing when the amount is more than the balance; otherwise takes the money
- `string Checkout(decimal amount)`: calls `Pay`. Returns `"Paid 30"` on success. If the wallet is short, **catches that** and returns `"Short by 12"`. Any other exception must **not** be caught.
- `Attempts` goes up by one for **every** call to `Checkout`, however it ends. That is a job for `finally`.
starter: public decimal Balance { get; private set; }
public int Attempts { get; private set; }
solution: public decimal Balance { get; private set; }
public int Attempts { get; private set; }
throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException("amount", "Amount must be positive");
template: Dojo.Check("InsufficientFundsException inherits from Exception", typeof(Exception).IsAssignableFrom(typeof(InsufficientFundsException)), "class InsufficientFundsException : Exception");
Dojo.Eq("the exception's Message is Short by 12", "Short by 12", dojoEx.Message);
Dojo.Try("Pay(30) leaves a Balance of 20", () => { dojoW.Pay(30m); Dojo.Eq("Pay(30) leaves a Balance of 20", 20m, dojoW.Balance); });
try { dojoW.Pay(32m); } catch (InsufficientFundsException dojoCaught) { dojoShort = dojoCaught.Shortfall; } catch (Exception) { }
Dojo.Eq("refused payments leave Balance at 20", 20m, dojoW.Balance);
Dojo.Eq("Pay alone does not count as an attempt", 0, dojoW.Attempts);
Dojo.Try("Checkout(5) returns Paid 5", () => Dojo.Eq("Checkout(5) returns Paid 5", "Paid 5", dojoW.Checkout(5m)));
Dojo.Try("Checkout(40) with 15 left returns Short by 25", () => Dojo.Eq("Checkout(40) with 15 left returns Short by 25", "Short by 25", dojoW.Checkout(40m)));
Dojo.Eq("Attempts is 3: success, shortfall and the uncaught one all count", 3, dojoW.Attempts);
hints: The exception class follows the card: a `Shortfall` property and a constructor ending `: base($"Short by {shortfall}")`.
`Pay` is two guard clauses and a subtraction. The missing amount is `amount - Balance`.
`Checkout` is `try { Pay(amount); return $"Paid {amount}"; } catch (InsufficientFundsException ex) { return $"Short by {ex.Shortfall}"; } finally { Attempts++; }`
